A sufficient trade relationship or other social and economic factors may exist which indicate that the area is commercially integrated with the base municipality, and if the geographic proximity requirement of the "adjacent to" language of section 203(b)(8) is met, the area should be encompassed within the commercial zone limits of the base municipality.
Our reliance on demographic trends and population studies in the Interim Report is criticized as not indicative of the commercial expansion of cities. First, we did not consider the demonstrated changes in population patterns as the determinative factor but only as one element of the evidentiary record. The original report in Ex Parte MC-37 took note of this interplay and certain incipient trends in the early post World War II years:
The war gave new impetus to the tendency of industrial establishments to locate in unincorporated areas adjacent to municipalities, with a consequent expansion of the area so occupied. Similarly, residential and emergency housing developments which, even when ostensibly temporary, have a tendency to become permanent, have been established somewhat more extensively than heretofore in areas adjacent to municipalities. Local transportation between such industrial and residential developments is of the type intended to be covered by the commercial zone exemption... Commercial Zones, 46 M.C.C. at 691.
